Q955.L1t: Hearsay is defined as an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter it asserts, and the rules of evidence provide a number of exceptions to the general bar on such statements.
Q955.L2t: A witness may testify to what they personally heard, and the same words can be hearsay or non-hearsay depending on the purpose for which they are offered.
Q955.L3t: The plaintiff is relaying his son's words only to show that the windows shattered, which indicates how big the explosion was, and a statement offered for something other than its truth is not hearsay, so no exception is needed and the son's availability does not matter.
Q955.L4t: The testimony is admissible regardless of whether the son can testify, because it is not hearsay in the first place.
Q955.L2f: The excited utterance exception requires that a statement be made while the declarant was still under the stress of a startling event, and it applies only if the declarant is unavailable to testify.
Q955.L3f: The son's words are an out-of-court assertion offered for their truth, so they count as hearsay, and they come in only if they qualify as a spontaneous excited utterance, which is doubtful because a child's remark about shattered car windows could reflect reflection and deliberation.
Q955.L4f: The testimony is inadmissible, because the son's statement cannot qualify as an excited utterance given that it could be a product of reflection and deliberation.

Q909.L1t: Good oral hygiene in patients who cannot care for themselves is an important part of basic nursing care.
Q909.L2t: Mouth care products have been compared in studies, and some commonly used agents can dry or irritate the oral mucosa when used repeatedly.
Q909.L3t: The recommended agent for cleaning the mouth is the one that is plain, non-irritating, does not dry the mucosa and does not alter the oral environment, and glycerine with lemon is acidic and drying, which makes it unsuitable.
Q909.L4t: Plain water is the recommended agent for cleaning the mouth.
Q909.L2f: Mouth care for dependent patients is recommended at least once a week, and the choice of cleaning agent has no effect on oral mucosal comfort or dryness.
Q909.L3f: Lemon and glycerine swabs stimulate saliva, moisturise the mucosa and are the gentlest agent available, so guidelines favour them over other solutions for cleaning the mouth.
Q909.L4f: Lemon and glycerine swabs are the recommended choice for cleaning the mouth.

Q884.L1t: Diplopia, or double vision, is a symptom caused by misalignment of the visual axes, and it is assessed by examining eye movements and the cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles.
Q884.L2t: Binocular diplopia disappears when one eye is covered, whereas monocular diplopia persists in the affected eye and usually has an ocular cause.
Q884.L3t: In a squint the image from the deviated eye falls on a non-macular part of the retina and is projected to the opposite side, and the image of the paralysed eye is the less distinct one, so the image seen furthest out is the one belonging to the affected eye.
Q884.L4t: The outer image is always the false image seen in diplopia.
Q884.L2f: Diplopia always has a central cause and is never produced by a problem with the muscles or nerves of the eye itself.
Q884.L3f: The sixth cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus, and its palsy leaves the medial rectus unopposed so the eye turns outwards, which is the picture of a divergent squint.
Q884.L4f: A sixth nerve palsy causes a divergent squint.
